- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then underestimates later — suggest adjusting for mean reversion toward recent history.
- When history shows a sharp spike (e.g., >90), model often overshoots and then undercorrects — apply a dampening factor or lagged smoothing to avoid overreaction.
- Forecast tends to be too optimistic in the first 3–5 days after a price drop — consider adding a “recovery lag” penalty or using a moving average of recent 7-day lows.
- Model frequently underestimates the true mean of the 30-day history — use a weighted average of recent 15–20 days as a baseline anchor.
- When true outcome is below forecast, model often fails to recognize the “bottoming” phase — add a downward bias correction if 3 consecutive days are below 85% of recent 7-day average.
- Forecast tends to be too volatile — apply a volatility cap or use a moving average filter to smooth out extreme swings.
- If the last 5 days of history are trending upward, model often fails to anticipate the continuation — adjust forecast to align with recent momentum, but not exceed 1.5x the recent 7-day average.
